title: Balancing Oncological Care and Quality of Life: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Strategies for Chemotherapy-Induced Cardiotoxicity—A Narrative Review
content: Background: Improving health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in patients undergoing chemotherapy has become a major therapeutic priority. Among the complications associated with cancer treatment, cardiotoxicity poses a considerable burden on both clinical outcomes and patient well-being. This review evaluates chemotherapy-related cardiotoxicity, focusing on the effects of early diagnostic modalities and cardioprotective interventions on HRQoL and patient-reported outcomes. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were explored using terms related to quality of life, cardiotoxicity, cancer, and chemotherapy. Studies were selected according to SANRA criteria. After duplicate removal, English-language studies involving adults undergoing chemotherapy were screened. Non-human studies, gray literature, and articles unrelated to chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity were excluded. Results: Of 1,149 records identified, 21 studies met the inclusion criteria, addressing either diagnostic methods or preventive strategies for chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity. Cardiotoxicity was associated with reduced HRQoL, particularly through fatigue and dyspnea. Cardiac MRI and echocardiography emerged as key tools for early detection, although evidence directly linking cardiac changes to HRQoL decline remains limited. Preventive strategies mainly included anthracycline- and trastuzumab-based therapies, exercise interventions, behavioral support, and nutritional supplementation. Physical activity and behavioral interventions consistently improved cardiorespiratory fitness and HRQoL, while limited evidence suggested potential benefits of L-arginine supplementation. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that exercise-based and supportive interventions may help preserve HRQoL in patients at risk of chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity. However, methodological heterogeneity and small study populations warrant further large-scale prospective research.
